title: How to Specify Non-Load-Bearing Studs for Interior Partition Walls
description: Learn how to choose non-load-bearing studs for partition walls by confirming load role, dimensions, deflection, performance, documents, and ordering details.
html:
Non-load-bearing studs frame interior partition walls, soffits, and ceilings and support wall finishes. They are not intended to carry primary building loads such as a floor, roof, beam, or other structural element.

Choosing the right product starts with confirming the wall’s function, then checking height, spacing, deflection, dimensions, finishes, documentation, and delivery requirements. This guide helps construction teams determine whether light gauge steel framing fits the application and prepare a complete supplier request.

Quick summary

  • Confirm that the wall supports partitions and finishes only, not primary building loads.
  • Identify the application, wall height, stud spacing, finish system, acoustic needs, and deflection condition.
  • Use project drawings and specifications to select the required stud width, length, profile, track, and related components.
  • Dass Metal documents widths of 1-5/8, 2-1/2, 3-5/8, and 6 inches, plus standard lengths of 8, 9, 10, and 12 feet. Custom lengths are also available.
  • Obtain project-specific review when structural, fire, acoustic, movement, or code requirements are unresolved.

Step 1: Confirm the wall is non-load-bearing

Begin with the architectural and structural drawings. Non-load-bearing steel studs frame a partition and support drywall or another finish, but they are not selected to carry primary building loads. They are commonly used for interior partitions, soffits, and ceilings. The stud wall basics can also help align framing terminology across the project.

Stop point: If the wall supports a floor, roof, beam, exterior load, or another primary structural element, do not specify it from this guide alone. Review the applicable structural design information, load tables, specifications, and qualified professional input. Canadian residential standards distinguish non-load-bearing partition studs from load-bearing steel studs, which require structural design under applicable provisions.

Step 2: Identify the partition, soffit, or ceiling application

Record where the framing will be used and what it must support. An interior partition may separate rooms and support gypsum board, while a soffit or ceiling arrangement may involve different geometry, access requirements, service coordination, and finish conditions.

Also note whether the wall is straight, contains openings, interfaces with other assemblies, or requires a particular head-of-wall condition. The application does not determine a universal stud size. It establishes the context for reviewing drawings, finish requirements, track arrangements, and related components.

Step 3: Review wall height, spacing, and deflection conditions

Wall height and stud spacing affect how a non-load-bearing steel stud supports its finish and responds to movement. Deflection expectations and the head-of-wall detail should be understood before the stud and track are released. Selection may also depend on acoustic requirements, structural requirements elsewhere in the assembly, and specified deflection head details.

Do not insert a guessed gauge, spacing, span, or deflection limit into the order. If the drawings do not identify these requirements clearly, consult the project specification, manufacturer documentation, applicable load tables, or a qualified design professional.

A taller partition, heavier finish, or movement-sensitive head condition may require a different profile or detailing approach than a short standard partition. These are design and coordination questions, not assumptions to settle from the product name alone.

Step 4: Select stud width and length from project requirements

Compare the required wall depth with the available product dimensions. Dass Metal documents non-load-bearing steel stud widths of 1-5/8 inches, 2-1/2 inches, 3-5/8 inches, and 6 inches. Standard documented lengths are 8, 9, 10, and 12 feet, with custom lengths available.

These dimensions are an ordering reference, not a universal recommendation. The selected width may need to accommodate insulation, services, the finish system, or a specified wall assembly. Confirm whether the project calls for a particular profile, gauge, coating, or other characteristic.

Length should reflect the framing layout, handling constraints, openings, and preferred installation method. If standard lengths do not suit the drawings or create unnecessary joints, ask whether a custom length is appropriate for the required profile, quantity, and schedule.

Step 5: Coordinate track, deflection, and related components

A steel stud wall is a system, so track and connection details should be coordinated with the studs. Confirm the required track type, width, length, and head-of-wall condition rather than ordering studs separately from the supporting details.

Standard track may suit a conventional partition, while a wall subject to expected movement may require a deflection-related detail. Do not assume that slotted deflection track, clips, or other accessories are interchangeable with every framing arrangement.

Confirm whether the project requires standard track, slotted deflection track, deep track, clips, bridging, or another component. The supplier request should identify the intended relationship between studs, track, deflection details, and finishes.

Step 6: Check acoustic, finish, and performance needs

Wall performance depends on the complete assembly, not only on the individual stud. Drywall type and layers, insulation, joints, penetrations, resilient components, and installation details may all affect the result.

If sound control is part of the brief, identify the required assembly and coordinate resilient channel or another acoustic component with the drawings and specifications. Do not describe a stud as automatically fire-rated, acoustically rated, or code-compliant in every application.

Confirm the tested, specified, or engineered assembly documentation for the particular project. Light gauge steel studs are cold-formed, zinc-coated members used primarily for non-load-bearing interior partitions, soffits, and ceilings.

Step 7: Verify drawings, standards, and local requirements

Before ordering, review the architectural drawings, structural drawings where relevant, wall schedules, specifications, product data, and required load tables. If the wall has fire-resistance, acoustic, height, movement, or occupancy requirements, ensure the documentation applies to the specified assembly.

For projects in Ontario, the Ontario Building Code provides provincial construction requirements. Use it alongside project drawings, specifications, permit documents, and professional design review. Code information does not replace confirmation of the exact wall assembly, product, or structural condition.

Requirements can differ by jurisdiction and project type. For work outside Ontario, confirm the applicable local requirements instead of carrying Ontario assumptions into another location.

Step 8: Prepare a complete supplier request

A clear request gives the supplier enough information to confirm the product and identify missing details. Include:

  • Application, such as interior partition, soffit, or ceiling.
  • Confirmation that the wall is non-load-bearing.
  • Wall height and required stud spacing.
  • Stud width, gauge or profile if specified, and required length.
  • Track type, including whether a deflection condition applies.
  • Openings, unusual geometry, service coordination, or special profiles.
  • Drywall, finish, acoustic, fire-performance, or other assembly requirements.
  • Quantity, handling considerations, and requested documentation.
  • Delivery location and the date material is needed on site.

Dass Metal Products manufactures non-load-bearing steel studs and track products and documents standard dimensions alongside custom-length availability. Complete information allows the request to be reviewed against the intended application instead of being treated as a generic request for steel studs.

Non-load-bearing studs compared with load-bearing framing

ConsiderationNon-load-bearing studsLoad-bearing framing
Primary roleFrame partitions and support finishes.Carry specified structural loads.
Common applicationsInterior partition walls, soffits, and ceilings.Applications identified by structural design, including load-bearing wall conditions.
Key informationWall height, spacing, deflection, width, length, track, finish, and assembly requirements.Structural loads, member design, connections, load paths, applicable design provisions, and engineering documentation.
Review pathConfirm product data and project specifications, then request the required dimensions and components.Follow structural drawings, design calculations, applicable standards, and qualified professional review.

Final ordering checklist

Before requesting a quote or releasing an order, confirm:

  • The wall is definitely non-load-bearing.
  • The framing application, wall height, and stud spacing are known.
  • Width, profile, gauge, and length are specified.
  • The head-of-wall condition and track type are confirmed.
  • Finish, acoustic, fire-performance, and service requirements are documented.
  • Quantity, documentation, and delivery location are included.

Stop and review: resolve structural, fire, acoustic, deflection, or code questions before finalizing the order. Non-load-bearing framing is not a substitute for primary structural framing or project-specific design.

Frequently asked questions

Can non-load-bearing steel studs support a floor, roof, beam, or other primary building load?

No. They are intended to frame partitions and support finishes, not carry primary building loads. If a wall has a structural role, use the project’s structural design and applicable load-bearing framing requirements.

What widths and lengths are available?

Dass Metal documents widths of 1-5/8, 2-1/2, 3-5/8, and 6 inches. Standard documented lengths are 8, 9, 10, and 12 feet, with custom lengths available. Confirm that the required dimension applies to the specific profile and order.

When should I use deflection-related track?

Use the detail identified by project drawings and specifications for the expected head-of-wall movement condition. Do not select slotted deflection track solely because it is available. Confirm the compatible stud, track, clip, and finish arrangement.

What information should I provide when requesting a quote?

Provide the application, non-load-bearing status, wall height, spacing, stud width and length, profile or gauge if specified, track type, deflection condition, finish and performance requirements, quantity, documentation needs, and delivery location.

Do non-load-bearing studs automatically provide a fire-rated or acoustic wall assembly?

No. Fire and acoustic performance applies to the complete specified assembly. Confirm the required wall system, product documentation, and project requirements rather than relying on the stud description alone.

Conclusion: Specify the wall before you specify the stud

The correct non-load-bearing studs depend first on the wall’s role, then on its application, height, spacing, movement condition, dimensions, track, finish, performance requirements, and documentation. Confirm those details before choosing standard sizes or requesting custom lengths.
